questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Oral cavity, salivary gland & pharyngeal disease
questions.stem: The commonest salivary gland tumour is:
questions.concept: Pleomorphic adenoma (benign mixed tumour) accounts for most salivary neoplasms, usually in the superficial lobe of the parotid, presenting as a slow-growing painless mobile swelling. Superficial parotidectomy is preferred over enucleation to avoid recurrence.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Oral cavity, salivary gland & pharyngeal disease
questions.stem: Facial nerve palsy in a patient with a parotid swelling suggests:
options: Malignant transformation or a malignant parotid tumour
questions.concept: The facial nerve passes through the parotid but is not affected by benign tumours; palsy, pain, fixity, rapid growth or cervical nodes indicate malignancy. FNAC and imaging are needed before surgery.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Oral cavity, salivary gland & pharyngeal disease
questions.stem: The commonest malignant salivary gland tumour is:
questions.concept: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is the commonest salivary malignancy overall, while adenoid cystic carcinoma is notorious for perineural spread, late distant metastasis to lung and poor long-term survival despite indolent growth.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Oral cavity, salivary gland & pharyngeal disease
questions.stem: Salivary calculi most commonly occur in the:
questions.concept: About 80% of salivary stones occur in the submandibular system because its secretion is more mucinous and alkaline with higher calcium, and Wharton duct drains uphill against gravity. Pain and swelling occur at mealtimes.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Oral cavity, salivary gland & pharyngeal disease
questions.stem: Frey syndrome following parotidectomy is characterised by:
options: Gustatory sweating and flushing over the cheek from aberrant parasympathetic reinnervation
questions.concept: Severed auriculotemporal parasympathetic fibres regenerate into sweat glands of the overlying skin, so eating provokes sweating and flushing. A positive starch-iodine test confirms it; botulinum toxin is the treatment of choice.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Oral cavity, salivary gland & pharyngeal disease
questions.stem: The commonest site of oral cavity carcinoma in India is:
options: The buccal mucosa and gingivobuccal sulcus, related to tobacco quid chewing
questions.concept: Gingivobuccal complex carcinoma is characteristic of Indian tobacco and areca nut chewing habits, sometimes called the Indian oral cancer. In Western countries the tongue and floor of mouth predominate.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Oral cavity, salivary gland & pharyngeal disease
questions.stem: Oral submucous fibrosis is strongly associated with:
questions.concept: Areca nut alkaloids cause juxta-epithelial fibrosis producing blanching, burning on spicy food and progressive trismus. It is a potentially malignant disorder with substantial risk of squamous carcinoma, so habit cessation and surveillance are essential.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Oral cavity, salivary gland & pharyngeal disease
questions.stem: Which oral lesion carries the highest risk of malignant transformation?
questions.concept: Erythroplakia, a velvety red patch, shows dysplasia or carcinoma in situ in most cases and carries far higher transformation risk than leukoplakia, so it must always be biopsied.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Oral cavity, salivary gland & pharyngeal disease
questions.stem: Adenotonsillar hypertrophy in a child may lead to:
options: Obstructive sleep apnoea with adenoid facies and cor pulmonale if severe
questions.concept: Chronic upper airway obstruction causes mouth breathing, adenoid facies with a high arched palate, hyponasal voice, sleep apnoea, failure to thrive and eventually pulmonary hypertension. Adenotonsillectomy is curative.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Oral cavity, salivary gland & pharyngeal disease
questions.stem: An absolute indication for tonsillectomy is:
questions.concept: Absolute indications include suspected malignancy, obstructive sleep apnoea from tonsillar hypertrophy and recurrent quinsy. Recurrent tonsillitis meeting the Paradise criteria is a relative indication.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: An extradural haematoma most commonly results from injury to the:
options: Middle meningeal artery with an associated temporal bone fracture
questions.concept: Rupture of the middle meningeal artery beneath a temporal fracture produces an arterial extradural collection, classically with a lucid interval, and appears biconvex (lens-shaped) on CT because it cannot cross suture lines.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A crescent-shaped hyperdense collection crossing suture lines on CT indicates:
options: Acute subdural haematoma from torn bridging veins
questions.concept: Subdural blood from torn bridging veins spreads across the whole hemisphere crossing sutures but not the midline, appearing crescentic. It is common in the elderly and alcoholics with cerebral atrophy and carries worse prognosis than extradural bleeds.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: The lucid interval classically described in head injury refers to:
options: A period of normal consciousness between the initial concussion and subsequent deterioration
questions.concept: The lucid interval is characteristic of extradural haematoma, as arterial blood slowly strips the dura before the mass effect causes deterioration and uncal herniation. Its presence demands urgent CT and evacuation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A Glasgow Coma Scale score of 8 or less indicates:
options: Severe head injury requiring intubation for airway protection
questions.concept: GCS 13 to 15 is mild, 9 to 12 moderate and 8 or below severe. A score of 8 or less means the patient cannot protect the airway and requires definitive airway management with neurosurgical referral.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Battle sign and raccoon eyes in a head-injured patient indicate:
questions.concept: Mastoid ecchymosis (Battle sign) and periorbital bruising (raccoon eyes) with CSF otorrhoea or rhinorrhoea and haemotympanum indicate basal skull fracture. Nasogastric tubes are avoided because of the risk of intracranial passage.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: The Monro-Kellie doctrine explains why:
options: Intracranial pressure rises steeply once compensatory displacement of CSF and venous blood is exhausted
Blood pressure falls with rising ICP
questions.concept: The cranium is a rigid box containing brain, blood and CSF; an expanding mass is first buffered by displacing CSF and venous blood, but once this reserve is exhausted, small further increases in volume cause steep rises in pressure.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Cerebral perfusion pressure is calculated as:
options: Mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure
questions.concept: CPP equals MAP minus ICP and should be maintained above about 60 mmHg. This is why hypotension is so damaging in head injury and why both raising MAP and lowering ICP are therapeutic goals.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Diffuse axonal injury is characterised by:
options: Immediate prolonged coma with relatively normal initial CT and petechial haemorrhages at grey-white junctions
questions.concept: Rotational acceleration-deceleration shears axons, causing immediate and prolonged unconsciousness with a CT that may look near-normal; MRI shows lesions at the grey-white junction, corpus callosum and brainstem. Prognosis is poor.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: The commonest cause of spontaneous subarachnoid haemorrhage is:
options: Rupture of a berry (saccular) aneurysm of the circle of Willis
questions.concept: About 85% of spontaneous subarachnoid haemorrhage is from a ruptured saccular aneurysm, presenting with sudden thunderclap headache, neck stiffness and photophobia. CT then lumbar puncture for xanthochromia confirms it; nimodipine prevents vasospasm.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A chronic subdural haematoma in an elderly patient typically presents with:
options: Fluctuating confusion, headache and progressive focal deficit weeks after trivial trauma
questions.concept: Cerebral atrophy stretches bridging veins so minor trauma, often forgotten, produces a slowly enlarging collection presenting weeks later with confusion, headache and gait disturbance. Burr-hole drainage gives excellent results.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: The rule of nines assigns what percentage of body surface area to an adult's entire lower limb?
questions.concept: In adults the head is 9%, each upper limb 9%, each lower limb 18%, anterior trunk 18%, posterior trunk 18% and perineum 1%. In children the head is proportionately larger and the limbs smaller, so the Lund-Browder chart is more accurate.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: The Parkland formula for fluid resuscitation in burns is:
options: 4 mL x body weight in kg x percentage burn of Ringer lactate in 24 hours, half in the first 8 hours
2 mL x weight x percentage over 24 hours
4 mL x weight x percentage of colloid
questions.concept: Parkland gives 4 mL/kg per percent burn of Ringer lactate over 24 hours from the time of injury, with half in the first 8 hours. Urine output of 0.5 to 1 mL/kg/hour is the best guide, as the formula is only a starting estimate.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A deep partial thickness (deep dermal) burn is characterised by:
options: Reduced sensation with a mottled appearance and sluggish capillary refill, healing slowly with scarring
Intact sensation with blistering and brisk refill
questions.concept: Superficial dermal burns are painful, blistered and blanch briskly, healing in two weeks. Deep dermal burns have diminished sensation and sluggish refill, heal slowly with scarring and often need grafting; full thickness burns are painless and leathery.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which finding suggests inhalational injury requiring early intubation?
options: Facial burns with singed nasal hair, soot in the oropharynx and hoarseness
A small scald on the hand
questions.concept: Airway oedema develops rapidly and unpredictably, so early elective intubation is safer than emergency intubation later. Carboxyhaemoglobin should be measured and 100% oxygen given, as pulse oximetry is falsely reassuring.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Escharotomy is indicated for:
options: A circumferential full-thickness burn causing distal ischaemia or restricting chest expansion
questions.concept: Inelastic circumferential eschar acts as a tourniquet as oedema develops, compromising limb perfusion or ventilation. Escharotomy incisions through the eschar down to fat relieve this and are performed at the bedside.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: The topical agent of choice for most burn wounds, with good eschar penetration limitations, is:
questions.concept: Silver sulfadiazine is widely used and painless but penetrates eschar poorly and may cause transient leucopenia. Mafenide penetrates eschar well, useful for cartilage-containing areas, but is painful and causes metabolic acidosis by carbonic anhydrase inhibition.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A split-thickness skin graft consists of:
options: Epidermis with part of the dermis
questions.concept: Split-thickness grafts include epidermis and a variable part of dermis, take more readily on imperfect beds and allow donor site re-epithelialisation, but contract more. Full-thickness grafts contract less and give better cosmesis but need an excellent bed.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: The commonest cause of death in the first 24 to 48 hours after a major burn is:
questions.concept: Massive capillary leak causes burn shock and death early if resuscitation is inadequate; beyond the first week, sepsis and multi-organ failure become the leading causes. Curling ulcer is a stress ulcer complication.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Marjolin ulcer is:
options: A squamous cell carcinoma arising in a chronic burn scar or long-standing sinus
A basal cell carcinoma of the face
questions.concept: Malignant transformation in a chronic unstable scar, ulcer or sinus produces a well-differentiated but locally aggressive squamous carcinoma after many years. Any non-healing or changing scar should be biopsied.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A skin graft fails to take most commonly because of:
options: Haematoma or seroma beneath the graft preventing plasmatic imbibition and revascularisation
questions.concept: Graft take depends on plasmatic imbibition then inosculation and revascularisation, all of which fail if a collection, shear movement or infection separates graft from bed. Meticulous haemostasis and immobilisation are therefore essential.
